title: Asset Acquisition or Business Combination? The ASC 805 Screen Test
summary: Asset acquisition vs business combination under ASC 805. See how the screen test works and what changes for goodwill and transaction costs.
body_markdown:
## Why the Classification Decides the Accounting


Asset acquisition vs business combination is the first question after a deal closes, and it decides the accounting for everything that follows. The answer turns on one thing. Whether the set you bought meets the definition of a business ASC 805 carries in its Master Glossary. That call is why indinero’s CPA team answers it during diligence, not at the first close after signing.


Classification isn’t a disclosure decision. It’s the accounting.


**Transaction costs flip direction.** A $400,000 stack of banker, legal, and valuation fees is an immediate operating expense in a business combination under ASC 805-10-25-23. The same fees capitalize into asset cost in an asset acquisition under ASC 805-50-30-1. Same cash, same quarter, opposite effect on reported earnings.


**Goodwill either exists or it doesn’t.** A business combination produces a residual under ASC 805-30-30-1 that carries impairment testing with it. Is there goodwill in an asset acquisition? No. ASC 805-50-30-3 says the cost allocation “shall not give rise to goodwill,” and that sentence is codification, not firm interpretation.


**The measurement period sits on one side only.** ASC 805-10-25-15 gives a business combination up to one year from the acquisition date to finish incomplete valuation work. An asset acquisition gets nothing. A later correction is an ASC 250 error.


Consequence Business combination Asset acquisition


Measuring what you bought Acquisition-date fair value, ASC 805-20-30-1 Cost allocated on relative fair value, ASC 805-50-30-3


Transaction costs Expensed as incurred, ASC 805-10-25-23 Capitalized into asset cost, ASC 805-50-30-1


Goodwill Residual, ASC 805-30-30-1 None, ASC 805-50-30-3


Contingent consideration Fair value at the acquisition date, ASC 805-30-25-5, remeasured through earnings when liability or asset classified Recognized when probable and reasonably estimable under ASC 450-20. Practice interpretation, ASC 805-50 is silent


Acquired IPR&D Fair value, indefinite-lived, regardless of alternative future use Expensed unless it has alternative future use, ASC 730-10-25-2(c)


Measurement period Up to one year, ASC 805-10-25-13 through 25-19 None. A later change is an ASC 250 error correction


Disclosure ASC 805-10-50, 805-20-50, 805-30-50 No dedicated ASC 805-50 package. Fall back to ASC 350-30, 360-10, 450-20


[FASB’s ASU 2017-01](https://storage.fasb.org/ASU%202017-01.pdf) narrowed the definition and has been fully effective for every entity for years. Treat it as settled law, not a new standard. What happens after the call is made sits in[post-acquisition accounting and integration](https://www.indinero.com/blog/post-acquisition-accounting-integration/) , and the wider picture in the[multi-entity accounting guide](https://www.indinero.com/blog/multi-entity-accounting-guide/) .


## The Screen Test for a Single Identifiable Asset


The ASC 805 screen test is a concentration ratio, and you run it before any judgment about operations. ASC 805-10-55-5A is the whole rule. If substantially all of the fair value of the gross assets acquired is concentrated in a single identifiable asset or a group of similar identifiable assets, the set is not a business and the analysis stops. The screen works in one direction only. Pass it and you’re done. Fail it and you’ve learned nothing.


### Getting the denominator right


The denominator is the fair value of the gross assets acquired, and the word gross is doing real work. Liabilities assumed are not deducted. ASC 805-10-55-5A takes three things out: cash and cash equivalents, deferred tax assets, and goodwill resulting from the effects of deferred tax liabilities. The same paragraph puts something back in. Any consideration transferred, plus the fair value of any noncontrolling interest and any previously held interest, in excess of the fair value of the net identifiable assets acquired. The premium you paid over identifiable net assets gets pushed into gross assets acquired, so nobody can engineer a pass by overpaying. Leave that line out and your ratio is overstated every time.


### What can be treated as one asset, and what can’t


ASC 805-10-55-5B combines assets that can’t be physically removed and used separately from another tangible asset without significant cost or significant diminution in utility or fair value. Land, a building, and property improvements are one identifiable asset on that logic, and an in-place lease intangible is combined with the related leased asset. The lease side of that combination runs through[ASC 842 lease accounting for private companies](https://www.indinero.com/blog/asc-842-lease-accounting-private-companies/) . ASC 805-10-55-5C then lists what can never be grouped as similar: a tangible and an intangible asset, intangibles in different major classes, a financial and a nonfinancial asset, financial assets in different major classes, tangible assets in different major classes, and assets in the same major class with significantly different risk characteristics. That last list is where most screen conclusions break.


### The 90 percent question, answered honestly


The codification does not define “substantially all” and does not state a percentage anywhere in ASC 805-10-55-5A. The roughly 90 percent figure circulating in practice is an interpretation in the Big Four guides, drawn from how the term reads elsewhere in GAAP.[Deloitte’s Roadmap on the definition of a business](https://dart.deloitte.com/USDART/home/codification/broad-transactions/asc805-10/roadmap-business-combinations/chapter-2-identifying-a-business-combination/2-4-definition-a-business) says the term is generally interpreted to mean 90 percent or more, then adds the sentence most articles drop. The FASB did not intend entities to treat it as a bright line. So 88 percent is not an automatic fail and 91 percent is not an automatic pass. Document the qualitative support either way, because “we were at 92 percent” is a number, not a memo.


## The Framework When the Screen Is Not Met


When the screen isn’t met, you test for substance. ASC 805-10-55-5 requires at minimum an input and a substantive process that together significantly contribute to the ability to create output, and ASC 805-10-55-3A routes you through paragraphs 805-10-55-4 through 55-6 and 805-10-55-8 through 55-9. The fork in that path is outputs.


### When the set has no outputs


The route narrows to one thing. ASC 805-10-55-5D requires the set to include employees who form an organized workforce with the skills, knowledge, or experience to perform an acquired process that, applied to another acquired input, is critical to the ability to develop or convert that input into outputs. Pre-revenue acquisitions turn almost entirely on whether people came with the deal and whether what they do is critical rather than administrative. The input that workforce converts can be intellectual property that could become a good or service, a resource that could be developed into outputs, or access to necessary materials or rights.


### When outputs already exist


ASC 805-10-55-5E gives four alternative criteria, any one of which establishes a substantive process: an organized workforce critical to continuing output, an acquired contract providing access to such a workforce, an acquired process that significantly contributes and can’t be replaced without significant cost, effort, or delay, or an acquired process that is unique or scarce. Then comes the trap. ASC 805-10-55-5F says the continuation of revenues alone proves nothing, and it excludes assumed customer contracts, customer lists, and leases where the set is the lessor. “We kept billing the same customers on Monday” feels like evidence of an operating business. The codification says it isn’t.


Two guardrails close the analysis. ASC 805-10-55-8 makes this a market-participant test, so your integration plan doesn’t turn a business into an asset group and the seller’s operating history doesn’t turn an asset group into a business. ASC 805-10-55-9 treats goodwill as an indicator that a substantive process was acquired, not a requirement.[PwC’s Viewpoint guide on the definition of a business](https://viewpoint.pwc.com/dt/us/en/pwc/accounting_guides/business_combination/business_combination__28_US/chapter_1_scope_US/12_definition_of_a_b_US.html) walks the same sequence. Where you take a partial stake instead of control, the prior question is[equity method vs consolidation](https://www.indinero.com/blog/equity-method-vs-consolidation/) .


## Accounting for an Asset Acquisition


Accounting for an asset acquisition is a cost accumulation and allocation model, not a fair value model.


1. **Accumulate cost.** ASC 805-50-30-1 and 30-2. Cash paid plus directly attributable third-party transaction costs. Internal costs, including your corp dev lead’s salary and any overhead allocation, stay expensed, so the memo needs that split.
2. **Measure each asset’s standalone fair value.** A valuation exercise, not an allocation.
3. **Allocate on relative fair value.** ASC 805-50-30-3 spreads cost across the individual assets acquired and liabilities assumed in proportion to their fair values. No residual line, no goodwill.
4. **Apply the allocation exceptions.** Where cost exceeds the sum of the fair values, practice keeps the excess off cash and other financial assets, off other current assets such as inventory, and off assets subject to recurring fair value or impairment measurement. That exception list is how the Big Four guides apply the 30-3 principle, because allocating excess onto a financial asset creates a day-two impairment.
5. **Handle the tax gross-up.** ASC 740-10-25-51 and the simultaneous equations method, where book and tax basis differ. The asset basis absorbs it, so there’s no earnings effect.


### A worked allocation, start to finish


You pay $10.0 million in cash and capitalize $350,000 of third-party legal and valuation fees, so cost is $10.35 million. Independent fair values come back at $7.0 million of developed technology, $2.5 million of customer contracts, and $1.0 million of equipment, totaling $10.5 million. Because fair values exceed cost, every asset is written down proportionately at roughly 98.57 percent of standalone fair value. Developed technology lands near $6.90 million, customer contracts near $2.46 million, equipment near $0.99 million. Nothing touches the income statement. No goodwill, no bargain purchase gain, no plug. Run it the other way and step four decides which assets absorb the excess.[KPMG’s asset acquisitions handbook](https://kpmg.com/kpmg-us/content/dam/kpmg/frv/pdf/2024/handbook-asset-acquisitions.pdf) works through the harder cases.


### Four fact patterns a growth-stage buyer will recognize


- **A competitor with its team and its customers, $14 million.** Twenty-two employees transfer and existing ARR continues. The screen fails because developed technology and customer relationships are different major intangible classes under ASC 805-10-55-5C, and criterion (a) of ASC 805-10-55-5E is met by the transferred workforce. Business combination.
- **A product and its code with no people, $3.2 million.** If substantially all the fair value sits in the developed technology, the screen is met and you stop. If it fails, a time-limited transition services agreement generally doesn’t convey ongoing access to a workforce. Asset acquisition in most fact patterns.
- **A book of 140 customer contracts, $1.8 million.** Same major class, similar risk, concentration at or near 100 percent. Screen met. Watch a book that mixes multi-year enterprise agreements with month-to-month SMB accounts, because those risk characteristics may not be similar.
- **A single building held in an LLC, $6.5 million.** ASC 805-10-55-5B combines the land, building, and improvements, and combines the in-place lease intangibles with the real estate. Screen met, directly analogous to Case A Scenario 1 of the ASU 2017-01 implementation examples at ASC 805-10-55-52 and 55-53.


That last one carries the point most write-ups miss. The GAAP answer is asset acquisition, and you still own an LLC. That entity has its own ledger, its own bank account, its own tax filing, and its own row in the consolidation. Your[multi-entity consolidation process](https://www.indinero.com/blog/multi-entity-consolidation-process/) and your[intercompany eliminations](https://www.indinero.com/blog/intercompany-eliminations-explained/) both grew, whatever ASC 805 called the transaction.


## Common Pitfalls


Each of these is a real failure mode that surfaces in diligence files and audit comment letters.


1. **Treating 90 percent as a rule.** Auditors ask for qualitative support at any ratio. A percentage without a documented rationale isn’t a position.
2. **Netting liabilities out of the denominator.** The screen uses gross assets acquired. Assumed debt doesn’t shrink it, and the only permitted combination is an unfavorable in-place lease liability with its leased asset.
3. **Forgetting to push the premium in.** ASC 805-10-55-5A requires the excess of consideration over net identifiable assets to enter gross assets acquired. Omit it and you manufacture a false screen pass.
4. **Treating continuing revenue as proof of a business.** ASC 805-10-55-5F says the opposite, and it’s the most common analytical error on the whole question.
5. **Letting intent drive the answer.** ASC 805-10-55-8 is a market-participant test. “We’re shutting down their back office” is not an input.
6. **Expensing deal costs in an asset acquisition.** Muscle memory from business combinations is wrong here. ASC 805-50-30-1 capitalizes directly attributable third-party costs.
7. **Assuming a measurement period exists.** It doesn’t. Finish the valuation before you close the books, not after.
8. **Conflating the GAAP classification with the tax structure.** A stock sale versus an asset sale is a separate analysis under the Internal Revenue Code. A deal can be a stock purchase legally and an asset acquisition for GAAP.
9. **Assuming one definition of a business.** For SEC registrants, Regulation S-X Rule 11-01(d) carries its own definition for Rule 3-05 and Article 11 purposes, and it isn’t the ASC 805-10 definition.


Two of these change shape when the seller is an affiliate. An acquisition from an entity under common control runs through[combined financial statements under common control](https://www.indinero.com/blog/combined-financial-statements-common-control/) instead of the acquisition method, and it becomes a disclosure event under[related party transaction disclosure](https://www.indinero.com/blog/related-party-transactions-disclosure/) . The[AICPA and CIMA guide on business combinations](https://www.aicpa-cima.com/cpe-learning/publication/accounting-and-valuation-guide-business-combinations) , finalized in November 2024, is what auditors most often cite back on the valuation work behind either path.

The classification memo is where transaction-processing bookkeeping breaks. A bookkeeper can record the wire. Building a screen-test calculation with the right denominator, documenting the ASC 805-10-55-5C major-class analysis, and writing a position that survives an audit is technical accounting work, and that’s why indinero’s accounting team is CPA-led. The deliverable isn’t a journal entry. It’s a defensible conclusion with the arithmetic attached.


You’re not just buying an accounting answer. You’re buying consistency across three answers that usually come from three different advisors.


The GAAP classification, the entity structure it leaves behind, and the tax position each run on different rules. When bookkeeping, GAAP close, business tax, and fractional CFO advisory sit in one monthly engagement, the screen-test memo, the new entity’s chart of accounts, the consolidation mapping, and the tax filing position all get built against the same fact pattern. That’s why the question belongs inside your[accounting services](https://www.indinero.com/services/accounting-services/) engagement rather than in a separate carve-out.


Timing is the other half. A business combination means engaging valuation specialists early. An asset acquisition means the fair values have to be final before the books close, because there’s no measurement period to catch you. Either way the entity doesn’t disappear. It gets opened in the ledger, intercompany accounts get set up, elimination entries get designed, and your[month-end close checklist](https://www.indinero.com/blog/month-end-close-checklist-saas/) gains a column.

## Frequently asked questions


These are the questions that come up once a deal is signed and someone has to book it. Each answer points back to the governing ASC paragraph, so you can take it straight to your auditor or your diligence team.


### Does an asset purchase agreement automatically mean an asset acquisition for accounting?


No, a deal papered as an asset purchase can still be a business combination under ASC 805. Legal form doesn’t decide the accounting. Run the screen at ASC 805-10-55-5A against the set you actually bought, then test for inputs and a substantive process if the screen isn’t met. The reverse happens too. An equity purchase of an LLC that holds one building is an asset acquisition for GAAP.


### Can a deal for a single product line or a customer list ever be a business combination?


Yes, if the fair value isn’t concentrated in one asset group and the set includes an input plus a substantive process. A customer list alone usually meets the screen, because the contracts sit in one major class with similar risk, and the analysis stops. A product line acquired with an organized workforce can satisfy ASC 805-10-55-5E. The 90 percent figure for substantially all is Big Four interpretation, not codification.


### Is there goodwill on the books after an asset acquisition?


No, an asset acquisition never produces goodwill, because ASC 805-50-30-3 states the cost allocation shall not give rise to goodwill. Cost gets spread across the individual assets acquired and liabilities assumed on a relative fair value basis, so there’s no residual line and no bargain purchase gain. Where cost exceeds total fair value, the excess loads onto the qualifying assets rather than a plug. The allocation itself never touches the income statement.


### How are the legal and advisory fees on the deal treated in each case?


Transaction costs are expensed as incurred in a business combination and capitalized into the cost of the assets acquired in an asset acquisition. ASC 805-10-25-23 drives the expense side. ASC 805-50-30-1 drives the capitalization side, and it covers directly attributable third-party costs only. Internal costs stay expensed, including your corp dev lead’s salary and any overhead allocation, so the memo needs that split documented before the books close.


### Does the classification change how the deal is reported on our tax return?


No, the GAAP classification doesn’t drive the tax treatment, because a stock sale versus an asset sale is a separate analysis. A deal can be a stock purchase legally and an asset acquisition for GAAP, with book and tax basis diverging from day one. ASC 740-10-25-51 handles the resulting gross-up in an asset acquisition. Building the GAAP memo and the return position on the same fact pattern is what prevents a mismatch later.


### Who should make the call, our accounting team or the valuation firm?


Your accounting team owns the ASC 805 classification conclusion, while the valuation firm supplies the fair value inputs the screen test runs on. Those inputs are only part of the answer. Someone still has to build the gross assets denominator, document the major-class analysis under ASC 805-10-55-5C, and write a position that survives review. That’s technical accounting work, which is why indinero’s CPA-led team writes the memo during diligence rather than after the close.


### What does an auditor ask for to support the classification?


Auditors ask for the screen test calculation, the qualitative support behind it, and a memo tying the conclusion to the governing ASC 805 paragraphs. Expect scrutiny on the gross assets denominator, specifically whether liabilities were netted out and whether the premium over net identifiable assets was pushed in. A percentage without documented rationale isn’t a position at any ratio. Where the screen isn’t met, they’ll want the input and substantive process analysis, not just continuing revenue.
